My dear Professor WiUcox: ,
.

hundredth birthday on March 22nd. I want to extend

Sincerely,

CENTENARIAN WILLCOX
Walter Francis Wilicox, Gamma '84,
Celebrates 1 00th Birthday
By HuBEKT C. Crowley, Gamma '59
PROFESSOR
WALTER FRANCIS
WILLCOX, Gamma '84, noted another
milestone in a
long and distinguished ca
reer on March 22, 1961. His 100th birth
day was marked by congratulatory letters
and telegrams from President John F. Ken
nedy and Governor Nelson A. Rocke
feller, Zeta '30, among countless others.
Although the birthday festivities in
cluded press interviews, a testimonial
luncheon by businessmen of Ithaca, and
a cocktaU party by Cornell faculty mem
bers. Brother WiUcox did not neglect his
daily two-mile walk.
FoUowing a custom of many years, he
divided the hike by going twice around
the block on which he lives near the hilly
Cornell campus and completing his exer
cise within his home. The inside track fol
lows a route starting in his bedroom, go
ing through the living room and around
the dining room table. Forty times around
the loop constitutes a mile, and this trim
and hearty brother keeps track of the laps
by turning coins on the table. "The body
is a machine and it should be kept in good
working order," he declares. "So 1 walk
regularly for the exercise."
The fact that he has reduced his daUy
walks to two miles, and that he needs a
magnifying glass to read fine print, appear
to be the principal concessions he has
made to his advanced age. His hearing
and perception are little impaired, and the
end of his first century finds him fully en
gaged in trying to reduce the Federal
Congress to a size which he considers
more conducive to efficiency.
While his friends and associates are
prone to look back over his distinguished
career as an economist, an educator and
a statistician, he himself is more concerned
with the years ahead, rather than those
behind. Credited with being largely re
sponsible for legislation more than three
decades ago which halted the steady
growth of membership in the national
House of Representatives, the professor
is now
trying to win support for another
proposal which would ehminate 137 per
sons from membership in that body. The
remaining 300 Congressmen would then
be able to do a better job than the pres
ent
unwieldy membership, he contends.
The elimination of the 137 Congressmen
would be accomplished gradually, at the
rate of ten every decade. Brother Wilicox
at age 100 is looking into the future
toward the year 2100 when Congress
would finally be reduced to 300 members,
if his proposal is accepted.
President Kennedy in noting Brother
Willcox's achievements stated, "I want to
extend to you my warmest, greetings as
well as the thanks of this government
for the many special services you have
performed over
your long career. I know
that the study of economics and statistics
in this country and the application of new
statistical techniques to public policy have
benefited enormously from your work."
Brother Wilicox received his formal edu
cation at Amherst College and Columbia
University and is the oldest living alum
nus of Amherst, and possibly of Columbia.
From Amherst he received the A.B. degree
in 1884, the A.M. in 1888, and the LL.D.
in 1906. From Columbia he received the
LL.B. and the Ph.D. degrees in 1887 and
1891 respectively.
A member of Phi Beta Kappa, he joined
the Cornell faculty in 1891 and in 1931
became professor emeritus. During his 40
years on the faculty, and the 30 years
since his retirement he has been one of
the nation's foremost statisticians.
At the end of the Spanish-American
War he served as a statistical expert for

the War Department in the taking of the
census in Cuba and Puerto Rico. He was
chief statistician of the Twelfth U. S. Cen
sus in 1900. His report appeared in 1906,
and he has remained an advisor to the
Census Bureau until recent years.
He has been president of the American
Economic Association, American Statisti
cal Association, World Statistical Congress,
and the International Statistical Institute.
He has been honorary president of the
latter organization since 1947. Several of
these groups held dinners in April honor
ing Brother Wilicox.
As Psi Upsilon's oldest living member,
it is fitting that a number of the chapters
can claim Brother Willcox's relatives as
members and benefactors from the earliest
years of the Fraternity to the present.
Brother Willcox's father, William H.
WUlcox, Delta '43, a
distinguished clergy
man, was
president of the Second National
Convention of the Fraternity in 1843
which was held at Union College. The pro
fessor's three sons, all Chi men and like
their father possessors of lengthy dossiers
in Who's Who in America, are: Bertram F.
'17, professor of law at Cornell; William B.
'28, professor of history at the University
of Michigan; and Alanson W. '22, general
counsel of the Department of Health,
Education and Welfare.
Three uncles of Brother WiUcox were
Giles B. WUlcox, Beta '48 and John H.
and Henry C. Goodenow of the Kappa
delegations of '52 and '53 respectively.
His brother was Howard H. Wilicox,
Gamma '89.
Brother Wilicox served as the senior
delegate from the Gamma to the 51st An
nual Convention of the Fraternity at the
Chi in May, 1884. Here he witnessed the
laying of the cornerstone of the Chi's first
real home, and the first fratemity house on
the CorneU campus.
Seventy years later on the occasion of
the 12Ist National Convention held at Cor
nell, members of the Chi presented a scroll
to Brother WUlcox which read: "Walter
Francis Wilicox, a member of the Gamma
Chapter and a
graduate of Amherst in
1884. During his 63 years of distinguished
service to Cornell University, he has been
actively interested in and associated with
the Chi Chapter, a rare
privilege for its
members and an
inspiration to us aU."
Brother Wilicox has also maintained his
ties with Amherst. He has served on the
Alumni CouncU of the coUege for many
years and was honored at his 75th reunion
in 1959 at the annual meeting of the
Society of the Alumni. He also visited the
chapter room of the Gamma and partici
pated in an informal discussion with sev
eral undergraduates about present-day col
lege activities.
President Calvin H. Plimpton of Am
herst summed up several attitudes in his
congratulatory message: "We are all tre
mendously proud of Professor Walter
Francis Wilicox. He is a beautiful example
of the motto of the Gerontology Society
of America�'Not merely add years to hfe,
but life to years.' He certainly is a re
markably lively person and he has our
heartiest wishes for continued good health
and vigor."
